When CarPlay was first released, I wasn’t interested, partly because of its limited availability. It was only found in newer cars from more exotic brands. That has changed; many new cars offer CarPlay connectivity, though there are some car companies that aren’t offering it.
Ever since I tried out CarPlay in my second car, I’ve come to view CarPlay more favorably. In fact, I’d hardly want to be without it now. However, my 2008 Renault Kangoo was made before CarPlay became a thing in 2014. The car was retrofitted with a Bluetooth receiver that uses the unused interface of the CD changer (the car really is old!). I’ve been able to listen to music from my iPhone through the car’s impressive sound system.
This is where the Lamtto RC37 Car Infotainment System comes into its own. Unlike other retrofit systems, it connects to the car’s stereo via Aux, FM, or Bluetooth. My car doesn’t have a 3.5-mm jack input, and FM transmitters only work locally at best, where you can still find a free frequency at the edges of the bands and they’re usually useless when on the move, requiring readjustment of the frequency for every transmission area.
More than just a CarPlay screen
The Lamtto comes with three further interesting features: a rear car camera (something my old car wouldn’t even have dared to dream of), a high-resolution 11-inch screen, and pre-installed entertainment apps.
You can stick the 11-inch display onto the dashboard or attach it to the windscreen using a suction cup. I opt for the suction cup, which makes the solution more flexible, as it’s removable, but it does obstruct the field of vision slightly–some may be able to quite literally, look past it. If I tilt the screen significantly lower or mount it on the shelf in front of the radio, I’ll lose sight of it. Sticking the stand on the passenger side is a bad idea because of the airbag. I’ll eventually find the right spot for it.
Setup is absolutely straightforward: switch it on, connect it to the iPhone, launch CarPlay, and you’re done. The Lamtto has a plug that fits into the cigarette lighter socket. This socket also features a USB-A port, which can be used to change and iPhone.
When operating the touchscreen, I found that the suction-cup mounting is less than ideal. The screen always gives way too much when touched. A stand would be the better solution, but then you have to consider a proper mounting area that  is accessible and doesn’t block your windshield. That’s more of a problem with the car and not with the Lamtto kit. At least, thanks to the Bluetooth connection, you can adjust the volume from the steering wheel. And, of course, the connected iPhone responds to Siri.
The system has TikTok, YouTune, and Netflix. They’re off-limits while driving, even if it’s the front passenger using them. Drivers can use them when the car is parked, but this is only of interest to anyone who takes longer driving breaks and whose car battery has sufficient charge.

				
					

				
			
The screen is a nice size, but it can be a bit of a nuisance in your field of vision.

Macwelt




Fiddly setup required for rear camera
The Lamtto’s rear camera is a feature that take it to a whole new level. This isn’t connected wirelessly, but via a cable to the Lamtto display. The manufacturer recommends mounting the camera on or above the license plate–a central position, close to the ground. You’ll need to figure out how to thread the camera’s cable through your car without it getting in the way of your windows or your doors.
The camera switches on automatically when the car is put into reverse. For this to happen you need to attach an additional cable to the positive terminal of the reverse lights of your car. When this lights up, the display receives a signal and shows the camera’s image. That setup is a bit too fiddly for me to do and I’d rather leave it to a professional, who’ll also help me position the display correctly in the car.
Within a very short time of turning on the ignition, the Lamtto device is ready to go, has launched CarPlay, found the iPhone, and resumed the music from where I last left off. Exactly how it should be.
Should you buy the Lamtto RC37? 
The Lamtto Car Entertainment System retrofits older vehicles with CarPlay and also offers a rear camera. The bright 11-inch display can also a disadvantage if you can’t find the right spot to mount it. If you have an 11-inch iPad, you can experiment with it in your car to see if the display would fit and where it wouldn’t get in the way.
Fitting the device in the car and setting it up is completely straightforward once you’ve chosen the right spot. Installing the rear camera requires a steady hand, the sort that car mechanics have.
The pre-installed entertainment apps such as YouTube, Netflix, TikTok and YouTube Music are of interest to those who take longer breaks (such as overnight) in a car park. Even in a traffic jam, and even if the screen is directed only at the front passenger or those in the back seats, watching videos in the car is strongly discouraged.

Well, we’ve found a solution: This Apple iPad 8th Gen is only $110 at Woot but if you use code APPLETEN, it’ll take off another 10 percent, bringing it under $100. It’s guaranteed to be free of major dents and dings, plus it comes with a 90-day warranty in cases there’s anything wrong with it.
For under $100, this older iPad model is an easy pick if you want a kid-friendly first tablet or a simple spare iPad for the house without paying full price.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Colors Buyer's Guide: Which Should You Choose?
content:
Apple's iPhone 18 Pro and ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max models come in four distinct color options, so which should you choose?


The ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ models come in Black, Silver, Glacier, and Burgundy. The aluminum and glass backs are more closely matched than on the iPhone 17 Pro, although the different materials remain somewhat visible.

You should also consider if you plan to use a case with your device and, if so, which one. The ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌'s large, full-width camera plateau stands out on most cases, exposing more of the device's color. Choosing a complimentary color should be your first priority. 

Burgundy

Burgundy is the most distinct and expressive ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ finish, and it is much darker than the ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro's equivalent Cosmic Orange. It looks closer to wine or plum than a vivid red.


Burgundy is the standout shade in the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ lineup, designed to be bold and attention-grabbing. It is the most noticeable ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ color, and the most likely to indicate that you have the latest generation device—there has never been an iPhone color option like it before. 

Burgundy Silicone and TechWoven cases if you want the phone and case to look closely coordinated. With a contrasting case, the large, exposed plateau becomes a prominent patch of red-purple. That is worth considering if you like to change between bright case colors: Burgundy will remain part of every combination.

MagSafe ring covers part of the back. Burgundy is the clearest way to distinguish this generation by color, but anyone hoping for a bright red iPhone may be disappointed. 

Choose Burgundy if you want a distinctive, dark color that remains noticeable even when the phone is in a case.

Glacier

Glacier is a cool, pale blue that gives the iPhone a much softer look than Burgundy. It is much lighter than the ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro's Deep Blue, yet it does not disappear into Silver; in-person, it still looks distinctly blue. 


Glacier is a useful middle ground if you want gentle color with some saturation, without making it the strongest feature of the phone. The exposed camera plateau gives an opaque case a light blue accent, while a clear case reveals most of the finish. Apple's clear case has a large white ‌MagSafe‌ ring, however, so it does not leave the back completely unobstructed.

Apple sells blue cases in shades such as Crisp Blue and Chambray Blue, but neither is named Glacier. If you want the case and phone to match precisely, it may be best to compare them in person; otherwise, a clear or neutral case lets Glacier stand on its own.

Choose Glacier if you want an iPhone with a fresh, subtle, and light appearance.

Silver

Silver is the most classic, versatile, and timeless option, but also the most practical. The finish gives off a clean and bright look that pairs well with virtually any case or wallpaper, and it reflects light more than the other three colors, making it quite neutral.


Its aluminum has a metallic sheen that leans toward white in some lighting conditions. This year, the two rear materials are the same tone, making the new model look much more cohesive than the two-tone Silver ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro.

Silver is also the most adaptable color for cases. The exposed silver plateau provides a crisp, light accent against a dark case and sits more quietly beside a pale one. The color is likely to age well since it goes well with any case and embodies Apple's most traditional colors.

It is also the only finish of the three that pairs well with Apple's own clear case. The clear case's white ‌MagSafe‌ ring is less of a visual interruption here than it is against Black or Burgundy. If you frequently change cases, Silver is unlikely to compete with your next choice.

Unlike Burgundy or Black, Silver minimizes the appearance of damage. When the anodized layer chips or scratches, the raw aluminum underneath is very close in tone, so imperfections blend in far better. For users who prioritize long-term durability of appearance, Silver is the most forgiving finish. It may not be as dramatic as Burgundy or as sleek as Black, but it is the safest choice for maintaining a "like-new" look over years of use.

Choose Silver if you want a classic, flexible look that mitigates the signs of damage.

Black

Black returns after the ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro offered Deep Blue as its darkest option. It offers a dark, neutral look without Deep Blue's blue cast.



A black case makes the exposed camera plateau blend into the rest of the phone. A light or colorful case has the opposite effect, framing a broad dark section across the top. Apple's clear case also makes its white ‌MagSafe‌ ring particularly noticeable against Black, so it is less suited to an uninterrupted all-black look.

If a deep chip or scratch exposes bare aluminum, its lighter color would stand out against this finish, especially on the plateau that Apple's cases leave uncovered. Anyone using the device without a case should be prepared for more noticeable damage. If visible marks would bother you and you plan to go without a case, Silver may be a better fit.

Choose Black if you want a dark, stealthy, and professional look, but be willing to accept signs of wear and tear.

title: Best time to buy AirPods in 2026: Buy now or wait?
content:
Macworld





If you’re planning to buy AirPods, timing your purchase can make a big difference to how much you pay. Apple rarely discounts AirPods itself, but retailers frequently cut prices – particularly around Amazon Prime Day and Black Friday.
October 2026 is an interesting time to buy because Apple has recently refreshed much of the range. The AirPods 5 launched in September 2026, joining the AirPods Pro 3, introduced in September 2025, and the AirPods Max 2, which arrived earlier in 2026. That means there is relatively little reason to wait for an imminent replacement if you want one of Apple’s current range of AirPods. 
There is, however, a very good reason to wait a few days if you’re reading this at the beginning of October: Amazon’s October Prime Day sale takes place on October 6 and 7, and AirPods regularly receive substantial discounts during major sales events. 
In this guide we’ll explain when the best time is to buy each AirPods model, whether you should buy now or wait, which older AirPods are worth considering at clearance prices, and the times of year when you’re most likely to find a bargain.

What is the worst time to buy AirPods?
The worst time to buy AirPods is generally immediately before a major sale, or just before Apple replaces the model you’re considering.
That’s particularly relevant right now. Amazon’s October Prime Day sale takes place on October 6 and 7, so paying full price for AirPods just a few days before the sale would make little sense unless you need them immediately.






What is the best time to buy AirPods?
Major sales events are generally the best time to buy AirPods. Amazon Prime Day and Black Friday are particularly worth watching because Apple’s headphones and earbuds frequently receive significant retailer discounts.
The savings can be substantial. AirPods Pro 3 have previously dropped from their $249 MSRP to $169, while AirPods Max 2 have already been available for $399 rather than $549.
That doesn’t mean you should never buy between sales. If the AirPods you want are already close to their historical low, there’s little reason to wait simply because another sales event will eventually arrive.






Should you buy AirPods now or wait? 
For most people, yes — but wait for Prime Day if you can

				
					

				
			
Foundry




For most people, October 2026 is a good time to buy AirPods – but wait until the October 6–7 Prime Day sale if you can.
Apple has recently refreshed the standard AirPods and AirPods Max ranges, while AirPods Pro 3 are only around a year old. That removes much of the risk that comes with buying immediately before a product refresh.
The bigger question is therefore not whether a new generation is about to arrive, but whether you can get the current model at a good price.
Read our AirPods Buying Guide to understand how the different AirPods compare and find out which is best for you. 







ModelOur advice

AirPods 5Buy, but wait for Prime Day if possible
AirPods Pro 3Buy, particularly when discounted
AirPods Max 2Buy only if you specifically want Apple’s over-ear headphones; look for a substantial discount
AirPods 4Clearance purchase only
AirPods Pro 2Consider only at a significant discount

 






Should you buy AirPods 5 now or wait?
Buy – but wait for a Prime Day discount if you can.
$129 at  Amazon										 | 
																$129 at  Apple										 | 
																$129 at  B&H						
					
The AirPods 5 only arrived in September 2026, so there’s little reason to wait for another generation. They are also much easier to recommend than the AirPods 4 they replace because Active Noise Cancellation is now standard.
AirPods 5 start at $129 with a USB-C charging case. Apple also sells a $149 version with a Wireless Charging Case, which adds wireless charging, a speaker for Find My, volume adjustment by swiping the stems and slightly longer battery life. 
The new generation also brings improved sound and stronger noise cancellation. Apple says AirPods 5 remove up to 50 percent more external noise than AirPods 4 with ANC. 
We think the $149 Wireless Charging Case version is the better choice for most buyers because it costs only $20 more and adds several useful features.
Our recommendation: Buy AirPods 5 if you prefer an open-ear design. If you aren’t in a hurry, wait until Prime Day on October 6–7 to see whether either version is discounted.






Should you buy AirPods Pro 3 now or wait?
Buy – particularly if you find them well below $249.
$234 at  Amazon										 | 
																$235 at  B&H										 | 
																$249 at  Apple						
					
AirPods Pro 3 launched in September 2025 and remain Apple’s most capable earbuds. They improve on AirPods Pro 2 with a more comfortable and secure fit, stronger noise cancellation, improved battery life and a heart-rate sensor.
They also have a significant battery-life advantage over AirPods 5, lasting up to eight hours with ANC enabled compared with four or five hours for the two AirPods 5 packages. AirPods Pro 3 additionally support Apple’s Hearing Test, Hearing Aid and Hearing Protection features.
Their $249 price is much higher than the $129/$149 AirPods 5, but discounts can dramatically narrow that gap. AirPods Pro 3 have previously fallen as low as $169, making sales events particularly attractive times to buy. 
Our recommendation: Buy if you want the strongest noise isolation, longer battery life, a secure in-ear fit or Apple’s health and hearing features. At full price, compare carefully with AirPods 5; at a substantial discount, AirPods Pro 3 become much more compelling.






Should you buy AirPods Max 2 now or wait?
Buy if you specifically want AirPods Max – but look for a discount rather than paying $549.
$479 at  Walmart										 | 
																$509.99 at  Amazon										 | 
																$509.99 at  Best Buy US						
					
AirPods Max 2 are relatively new, so waiting for an imminent replacement isn’t the main concern. The bigger issue is value.
The second-generation model adds the H2 chip and features including Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Voice Isolation and Live Translation. Sound quality, Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency mode remain excellent. 
However, our review found that Apple failed to address several longstanding complaints, including the headphones’ weight, Smart Case and inability to be switched off manually.
That makes the price particularly important. AirPods Max 2 cost $549, but the updated Prime Day roundup has already recorded a $399 deal – $150 below MSRP. 
Our recommendation: Don’t wait because – Apple isn’t expected to update the AirPods Max soon. Instead, wait for a good discount unless you particularly want them immediately.






Should you buy AirPods 4?
Only at a substantial clearance discount.
$89 at  Walmart										 | 
																$149 at  B&H										 | 
																$149.99 at  Best Buy						
					
AirPods 5 have replaced AirPods 4 and now include Active Noise Cancellation as standard while starting at the same $129 MSRP previously charged for AirPods 4 without ANC.
That makes older AirPods 4 difficult to recommend unless retailers cut their prices significantly. The standard model fell to $99 during Prime Day, but now that AirPods 5 cost $129, we’d want to see an even lower clearance price before choosing the older generation.
Our recommendation: Buy the ANC equipped version only  if the price is exceptionally low.






Should you buy AirPods Pro 2?
Only at a significant discount.
$173.99 at  Walmart										 | 
																$248.96 at  Best Buy US										 | 
																$249 at  Apple						
					
AirPods Pro 2 are still capable earbuds, but AirPods Pro 3 improve the fit, battery life and noise cancellation and add heart-rate sensing. 
The older model can still make sense if retailers are clearing stock at a sufficiently low price. But the closer its price gets to a discounted pair of AirPods Pro 3, the less attractive it becomes.
Our recommendation: Consider AirPods Pro 2 only if they’re substantially cheaper than AirPods Pro 3 and you don’t need the newer model’s heart-rate feature.






Should you buy older or refurbished AirPods?

				
					

				
			
Screenshot

Foundry




Older AirPods can make sense when retailers are clearing stock, but compare the price with the model that replaced them rather than focusing on the percentage discount from the original MSRP.
You should also be careful when buying an older generation simply because it appears heavily discounted. The percentage saving can be misleading if the replacement model offers significantly more for a similar price. AirPods 5, for example, start at the same $129 price originally charged for AirPods 4 without ANC, but now include Active Noise Cancellation as standard.
You should be particularly cautious when buying AirPods from marketplaces or unfamiliar sellers. Counterfeit AirPods can closely resemble genuine products, and unusually low prices – particularly on second-hand marketplaces – can be a warning sign. 
If you’re considering an older model, check the exact generation, charging case and condition, and make sure the seller is reputable.






When does Apple release new AirPods?
Unlike the iPhone, AirPods don’t follow a simple annual update schedule.
AirPods Pro 3 launched in September 2025, AirPods Max 2 followed in 2026, and Apple introduced AirPods 5 in September 2026. 
Because the three main AirPods families have all been updated relatively recently, the current lineup doesn’t present the obvious “wait because a replacement is imminent” problem that sometimes occurs with Apple products.

title: More evidence emerges of an imminent Apple device launch
content:
Macworld





Following a report Wednesday that Apple is planning to launch three new smart-home products on October 13, more evidence has emerged to indicate that something is indeed coming soon. According to a report from MacRumors, Apple retail stores have received packages that aren’t to be opened until October 8.
The site claims it has multiple sources that confirm Apple Stores “around the world” have received “confidential” boxes with instructions to not open them until October 8. The boxes appear to contain “new visual merchandise, which enables workers to update labels, graphics, and product layouts in stores around the release of new products.”
Of course, Apple is also launching the iPhone Duo this month, with in-store availability beginning on October 23. However, as MacRumors notes, it’s unlikely that there would be secrecy around those displays, as the product has already been announced and new store displays are very much expected to go up around that time.
We’ve heard about stores receiving displays ahead of events and launches before, but it’s rare for Apple Stores to get information about new devices before the general public. So if the report is accurate, a date of October 8 would indicate that Apple plans to announce something next week rather than, or in addition to, October 13.
It’s also worth noting that Apple Stores don’t generally advertise new products until they’re available for purchase or at least on display. So if stores are changing their signage for October 9, it would indicate that something new will be available. 
Apple is expected to launch at least three new smart-home devices, including an updated Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini, as well as a new smart-home hub. It’s not uncommon for Apple to space out announcements on multiple days when there isn’t an official event.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Aperture Control Goes Fully Manual in Halide 3.2
content:
Award-winning camera app Halide Mark III has been updated to version 3.2, bringing dedicated support for iPhone 18 Pro by broadening user control over the device's new variable aperture camera system.


Apple's stock Camera app lets iPhone 18 Pro owners choose from a four-stop variable aperture ranging from ƒ/1.48 to ƒ/4.0, delivering around 50 percent better low-light performance and giving users more optical control over depth of field.

Halide 3.2 does away with that four-stop limitation and instead lets you select any ƒ-stop setting within the camera's full range. 

There are two styles of aperture control in the app. The first is Aperture Priority mode, where you can set the ƒ-stop and the app handles the shutter speed and ISO to properly expose the shot.

The other style is Manual mode, which gives users full control over all three settings. This includes ISO settings – something that Apple's stock Camera app doesn't offer manual control over. Halide has said it is also considering adding f-stop presets in future updates, based on user feedback. 

this update though, Halide 3.2 adds two new film simulations, or photographic looks: Dawn and Quicksilver. Dawn features "filmic warmth in mid-tones and highlights, paired with rich yet gentle shadows and subtle complementary cool colors." 

Quicksilver is described as a "high contrast and muted color" that simulates a "silver-retention alternative process." Halide's developers call it an "excellent midpoint between color and stark black-and-white."

Lastly, version 3.2 introduces a new 16:9 aspect ratio shooting mode for those who want to use a wider framing.
iPhone 18 Pro: Using the New Variable Aperture Lens

download on the App Store, and costs $69.99 as a one-time purchase price, or $19.99 for an annual subscription.

title: iPhone Duo Guide: Everything you need to know about Apple’s folding iPhone
content:
Macworld





The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone, will be available to pre-order on October 16 and goes on sale October 23. Buyers can begin Apple’s “Get Ready” process on October 12, allowing them to choose their configuration and prepare payment, trade-in and delivery details before orders officially open.
The Duo opens like a book from a compact 5.4-inch phone into a much larger 7.6-inch device. Apple describes the internal screen as its largest-ever iPhone display, with 50 percent more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, while the outer display provides more than 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro.
The biggest change is obviously the folding design, but Apple has done more than simply add a hinge. The iPhone Duo will ship with iOS 27.1, which adapts to different positions and orientations with fold-specific interface and multitasking features. These include Split View, hands-free FaceTime and video, StandBy without charging, and layouts that move seamlessly between the two screens. Apple Pencil USB-C support is also coming later in 2026.
The other major changes are the 7.6-inch nano-texture inner display, Touch ID replacing Face ID, an A20 Pro processor with vapor-chamber cooling, and a dual-battery system designed around the two halves of the phone. Apple has also introduced camera features that exploit the second screen, including Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and Duo FaceTime.
Much of the pre-launch reporting proved accurate: the Duo name, book-style design, roughly 7.7- and 5.4-inch screens, Touch ID, two 48MP rear cameras, two front-facing cameras, A20 Pro, C2 modem, MagSafe and the white/dark-blue colours were all anticipated.
iPhone Duo at a glance
Apple’s first folding iPhone, with 5.4-inch outer and 7.6-inch inner displays.
Touch ID replaces Face ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button.
A20 Pro with vapor-chamber cooling, including a new 2nm manufacturing process.
Dual-battery architecture, giving up to 44 hours of video playback on the outer display.
Fold-specific iOS and camera features, including Split View, Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and hands-free use.
iPhone Duo: Top 10 features


Foldable designBook-style titanium design with precision hinge
Inner display7.6-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz ProMotion
Outer display5.4-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz ProMotion
ProcessorA20 Pro, 6-core CPU, 7-core GPU
Neural EngineDual 16-core Neural Engine
AuthenticationTouch ID in side button
Rear cameras48MP Main + 48MP Ultra Wide
BatteryDual batteries; up to 44 hours video on outer screen
ConnectivityC2 modem, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, second-gen UWB
Storage256GB, 512GB, 1TB or 2TB

 






iPhone Duo release date: When will it go on sale?
Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo on September 9, 2026, but unlike the iPhone 18 Pro models it won’t arrive until October.
From Monday, October 12, Apple will let customers “Get Ready” for iPhone Duo pre-orders. Through the Apple Store app, buyers will be able to choose their preferred color and storage capacity, select a carrier, arrange a trade-in or financing, choose AppleCare+, and enter payment and delivery information in advance. That should make placing the final order considerably quicker once pre-orders open.
Pre-orders begin on Friday, October 16, at 1 p.m. in the U.K. and 5 a.m. Pacific in the U.S. 
The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale one week later on Friday, October 23, in more than 70 countries and regions, including the U.S., U.K., Canada, Australia, China, France, Germany, India and Japan. A further 28 countries and regions will get it on October 30.
Pre-order iPhone Duo at Apple U.S. 
Pre-order iPhone Duo at Apple U.K. 
It will be available directly from Apple online and through Apple Stores, with carrier availability varying by market.
Initial supplies may be limited. A late-September supply-chain report claimed Apple and its manufacturing partners were still experiencing relatively low production yields for the new folding design. 






iPhone Duo design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			
The iPhone Duo opens up like a book.

Apple




The iPhone Duo uses a book-style folding design. Closed, it is unusually short and wide for an iPhone, measuring 84.1mm wide, 117.8mm tall and 11.3mm thick. Open it and the width expands to 164.6mm, while thickness reduces to just 5.2mm, making it Apple’s thinnest iPhone when unfolded (taking that mantle from the iPhone Air). It weighs 254g.
The outer screen measures 5.4 inches, while the folding inner panel measures 7.6 inches. Both are Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz, Always-On display support and up to 3,000 nits outdoor peak brightness. The internal display also has a nano-texture surface designed to reduce reflections and make the crease less noticeable.
The frame and hinge cover are made from Grade 5 titanium. Apple uses a mirror-polished finish on the enclosure and a micro-blasted finish on the 3D-printed hinge cover. Ceramic Shield protects the rear, while Ceramic Shield 2 protects the outer display. The phone retains an IP68 rating despite its folding construction.

				
					

				
			
The hinge from the outside.

Apple




There are just two colors: Star White and Night Sky, essentially confirming the pre-event reports of silver/white and a very dark blue. For more information read about the iPhone Duo colors.
Action button and Camera Control
There is Camera Control, giving access to exposure, depth, zoom, cameras, styles and tone. It can also launch the new Siri Camera mode.
However, Apple’s Duo doesn’t feature an Action button. The regular iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max retain both the Action button and Camera Control, so this is one hardware-control compromise of the folding model.
Accessories
Apple is also launching two dedicated accessories for the foldable: 
The iPhone Duo Case at $79/£79
The Duo Folio with Kickstand at $129/£129
Both will be orderable from October 16.






Face ID, Touch ID and the notch
Perhaps the most surprising difference between the iPhone Duo and Apple’s other flagship iPhones is that there is no Face ID.
Instead, Apple has brought back Touch ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button. It works whether the Duo is folded or unfolded, and Apple Watch can also be used to unlock the device. This confirms one of the most persistent pre-launch rumors.
The internal display therefore does not need the TrueDepth sensors used for Face ID. Its FaceTime camera sits beneath the display and disappears when it isn’t being used, giving the inner screen a largely uninterrupted surface.
The inner camera itself is hidden below the display rather than sitting permanently in a visible camera cutout. And yet, despite this and the absence of Face ID, there is still support for Dynamic Island.





iPhone Duo cameras: What cameras does it have?

				
					

				
			
There are two cameras on the rear.

Apple




The Duo has a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system, comprising:


CameraResolutionEquivalent focal lengthAperture

Fusion Main48MP26mmf/1.6
2x crop from Main12MP52mmf/1.6
Fusion Ultra Wide48MP13mmf/2.2
Outer front camera12MP—f/2.2
Inner FaceTime cameraApple does not specify resolution—f/1.8

 



The Duo does not have variable aperture. Variable aperture is exclusive to the 48MP Fusion Main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.


The biggest camera features for iPhone Duo
Duo Preview
The outer screen can show a live preview while somebody else is being photographed, allowing the subject to adjust their pose and framing.
Smart Take and Kid Cue
Smart Take detects when everybody is ready and automatically captures the shot. Kid Cue uses animations on the outer screen to encourage children to look towards the camera.
Two-screen shooting
The folding design supports unusual shooting configurations, including using the main cameras for selfies or group photos while seeing the composition on the other screen. Duo FaceTime can also put nearby participants onto the outer display.
Other notable camera features include 48MP macro photography, a 2x optical-quality crop from the Main camera, an under-display inner FaceTime camera, Dual Capture for simultaneous front-and-rear video, and 4K Dolby Vision recording at up to 120fps.






Rear cameras
The 48MP Fusion Main has an f/1.6 aperture, sensor-shift stabilization and can shoot 24MP or 48MP images. It also provides a 12MP, 2x optical-quality crop equivalent to a 52mm lens.
The 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide has a 13mm-equivalent lens, f/2.2 aperture and 120-degree field of view. It also supports 48MP macro photography and is the same Ultra Wide camera used by the iPhone 18 Pro family.
That means the Duo does not match the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max camera system. Those phones add a dedicated 48MP Fusion Telephoto and variable aperture on the Main camera, making the Pro models much more flexible for photography despite costing substantially less.
Pre-event reports were divided between a Main + Telephoto and Main + Ultra Wide arrangement. Apple ultimately chose Main + Ultra Wide, confirming the earlier reports that a dedicated telephoto could be sacrificed to save space.
Front cameras
On the outside is a 12MP Center Stage camera with an f/2.2 aperture. It supports Center Stage, automatic portrait/landscape framing, Dual Capture, Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5 and 4K Dolby Vision video at up to 60fps.
Inside is an under-display FaceTime camera with an f/1.8 aperture. Apple does not specify its megapixel resolution. It supports Center Stage for video calls and records at up to 1080p/60fps. Its major advantage is visual rather than photographic: the camera effectively disappears beneath the display when it isn’t being used.
iPhone Duo video features
The Main camera records 4K Dolby Vision at 24, 25, 30, 60, 100 or 120fps, with 4K/120fps also available for slo-mo. Cinematic mode reaches 4K/60fps and Action mode up to 2.8K/60fps. Dual Capture can record at up to 4K/30fps.
Apple’s specifications also do not list ProRes or Apple Log recording for the Duo. Those remain more Pro-oriented capabilities rather than part of Apple’s foldable camera proposition.
The Duo does support Spatial Audio recording, Audio Mix, Dolby Vision HDR and Apple’s computational photography features including Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5, Photographic Styles 3, smart focus tracking and Apple Intelligence-powered editing.
Apple does not list conventional Spatial Video capture in the Duo specifications.






iPhone Duo processor: What processor does it use?

				
					

				
			
Watch video on the screen.

Apple




The iPhone Duo uses the A20 Pro, the same processor as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, a major step forward in transistor density and efficiency. Apple combines it with a new chip packaging design inspired by its M-series Mac processors. The package connects the A20 Pro directly to a custom vapor chamber to transfer heat away from the processor more effectively.
The A20 Pro includes:
6-core CPU: two super cores and four efficiency cores
7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators
Dual 16-core Neural Engine
Hardware-accelerated ray tracing
A dedicated display engine capable of operating both Duo displays
Compared with the A19 Pro, Apple says the CPU is up to 20 percent faster, while the GPU is up to 40 percent faster and more power-efficient. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers twice the compute power, while unified-memory bandwidth rises by 50 percent.
Apple also claims that the complete thermal system gives the Duo up to 35 percent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro. That sustained-performance figure is particularly important for a folding device because prolonged gaming, multitasking and AI workloads generate considerably more heat than short benchmark bursts.






iPhone Duo RAM: How much memory does it have?
Apple has not disclosed how much RAM is inside the iPhone Duo.
Before launch, supply-chain reports consistently pointed to 12GB of RAM, which would make sense given the demands of running two displays, simultaneous applications, Siri AI and larger on-device AI models. 
Apple does reveal that A20 Pro has 50 percent more unified-memory bandwidth than A19 Pro, which should help the Duo move data more quickly between the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine.
Extra memory is particularly useful on the Duo because iOS 27.1 can display multiple apps simultaneously and because Apple Intelligence and Siri AI increasingly run generative models locally rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.






iPhone Duo connectivity

				
					

				
			
An expensive desk calendar. 

Apple




Apple has put a significant amount of its own communications silicon into the iPhone Duo.
It uses Apple’s new C2 cellular modem, replacing Qualcomm silicon. Apple says C2 introduces AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability and supports mmWave 5G in the U.S.
The N1 wireless networking chip provides:
Wi-Fi 7 with 2×2 MIMO
Bluetooth 6
Thread networking
The USB-C port also supports USB 3 data transfers at up to 10Gbps and DisplayPort video output.
The Duo also has Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, NFC and precision dual-frequency GPS.
It is eSIM-only worldwide, something that had been widely rumored before launch. Eliminating the SIM tray gives Apple additional internal space for its batteries.
Satellite capabilities include:
Emergency SOS via satellite
Roadside Assistance via satellite
Find My via satellite
Messages via satellite






Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s available?
Instead of one battery spanning the body, the iPhone Duo contains two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, with one high-energy battery fitted into each half of the device. Apple’s energy-balancing algorithms make them operate as a single battery system.
Apple rates battery life at:
Up to 24 hours of typical use
Up to 44 hours video playback using the outer display
Up to 31 hours using the inner display
Up to 37 hours streamed video on the outer screen
Up to 26 hours streamed video on the inner display
Apple has not disclosed the batteries’ combined capacity in mAh. The pre-launch rumor of approximately 5,000-5,500mAh therefore remains unconfirmed.
Wired charging can take the Duo to 50 percent in around 20 minutes with a 60W-or-higher USB-C adapter.
Despite earlier uncertainty, MagSafe is supported, with wireless charging at up to 25W. Qi2 charging also reaches 25W. Apple says a 35W-or-higher adapter and MagSafe charger can bring the battery to around 50 percent in approximately 30 minutes.





iPhone Duo price: How much does it cost?
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the U.S. and £1,999 in the U.K. for 256GB.
Prices are:


StoragePrice

256GB$1,999/£1,999
512GB$2,199/£2,199
1TB$2,599/£2,599
2TB$3,199/£3,199

 



The 256GB starting capacity means Apple has not created an unusually low-storage entry model simply to make the headline price look lower.


iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro pricing
The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. That makes the Duo approximately $700/£700 more expensive than the Pro Max at entry level.
That premium buys the folding display, precision hinge, titanium structure, second screen and more complex dual-battery design rather than superior cameras: in several areas the iPhone 18 Pro models are actually better equipped.
Reports before the launch suggested the Duo could cost anywhere from around $1,999 to $2,399 at entry level, largely because of the folding OLED display, hinge mechanism, titanium components and other expensive parts. Apple ultimately landed at the very bottom of those predictions.






Should you buy the iPhone Duo?
The iPhone Duo is the iPhone to buy if you genuinely want a phone and small tablet in one device. Its 7.6-inch display, multitasking features, A20 Pro performance and clever fold-specific camera modes offer capabilities no other iPhone has. 
But at $1,999/£1,999 it is enormously expensive, and there are significant compromises: no Face ID, no dedicated telephoto camera, no variable aperture and no Action button. 
For photography, battery life and conventional everyday use, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is likely to be the better-value flagship. Buy the Duo because you want the folding experience, not because it is simply the “best” iPhone.

title: How much power does the iPhone’s always-on display really use?
content:
Macworld





The always-on display is a brilliant feature, particularly on the Apple Watch, where it makes the smartwatch look just like a proper watch. With the iPhone 14 Pro, Apple began incorporating a similar technology into the iPhone. Starting with the iPhone 17, Apple included the always-on display on all models except the iPhone 17e.
But how does the always-on display affect an iPhone’s battery life? After all, the battery has to power the large screen almost constantly. There are situations where the always-on display is switched off, despite the setting being enabled: in Sleep mode, when the iPhone is lying face down, when a paired Apple Watch isn’t nearby, or when CarPlay is activated in the car.
I ran a few tests to compare battery life when the always-on display is activated, and compared the results to when the display turns off when it’s not in use. Surprisingly, the results aren’t as drastic as one might think.
Testing battery life
My two weeks of testing involved an iPhone 17 running iOS 27 Beta 3. In the first week, I used the iPhone daily with the always-on display. In the following week, the screen was switched off. From the recorded data, I extracted the battery statuses at 15-minute intervals for each day and categorized them as Always On and Always Off. This yielded 672 data points in each category.

Effect of always-on display on the iPhone battery

Foundry


If you filter out the rows in both datasets showing the battery level when the iPhone was being charged, and calculate the discharge rate per hour, it turns out that the iPhone discharges at an average rate of 4.27 percent per hour when the display is always on. For an iPhone with the display deactivated, this rate is 3.75 percent per hour. The discharge rate during the day, from 8 a.m to 11 p.m., was 5.88 percent with the always-on display activated, and 5.37 percent with it off.
As can be seen from the data in the graph above, both discharge curves run almost parallel. There are no major discrepancies between the different settings that would suggest the always-on display being switched off has a significant effect on battery life. The t-test, which precisely calculates the significance of a factor, also yields a p-value of 0.3011 in this case. Significance is established at a p-value of 0.05 or less. This means that whether the always-on display is enabled or disabled has no significant effect on battery life.
Our measurement data supports what Apple claimed when introducing the always-on display in 2022. When the screen is locked, it is throttled down to 1Hz, which reduces power consumption. In the chaos of everyday life, which is influenced by user behavior, signal strength, and outside temperatures, whether the screen is on or off does not make a significant difference.

title: New HomePod rumors: HomePod mini 2, HomePad and touchscreen HomePod
content:
Macworld





Apple’s HomePod lineup could be about to undergo its biggest expansion since the original HomePod launched. Apple is reportedly preparing a new HomePod mini and smart home display for October 13, with another full-size HomePod expected further down the line, as it builds a new generation of home products around Siri AI.
For much of 2025 and 2026, Apple’s revamped Siri was the thing holding those products back. That’s no longer the case: Siri AI has now arrived with Apple’s OS 27 updates, removing one of the biggest obstacles to launching the new hardware. The HomePod mini 2 appears to be particularly close, with Apple code discovered in September 2026 revealing images of the unreleased speaker and its five colors, while Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in July that a new HomePod mini, Apple TV and smart home display are among Apple’s upcoming home products.
The naming is less straightforward. “HomePad,” “Smart Home Hub,” “Personal Hub” and “HomePod Touch” are all placeholder names being used for different rumored products or concepts, rather than confirmed Apple names. In this article, we’re using “HomePad,” “Smart Home Hub” and “Personal Hub” for the standalone smart display reportedly being developed for smart-home controls, Siri AI and video calls, while “HomePod Touch” refers specifically to reports about a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated touchscreen.
There may ultimately be some overlap between these products, and some of the rumored concepts could be combined, renamed or never released at all. Below, we separate what is currently known about each device and when it is likely to arrive.







What are the new HomePod products?
Apple is reportedly developing several new HomePod and smart-home products. The names below aren’t official Apple names; where necessary, we’re using placeholder names to distinguish between the different rumored devices.


Placeholder nameWhat is it When 

HomePod mini 2New HomePod mini with the same basic design, new colors, faster processor and Siri AI support.October 13, 2026 (rumored)
HomePad/Smart Home Hub6-inch smart display with Siri AI, Home controls, apps and camera; tabletop and wall-mounted versions expected.October 13, 2026 (rumored)
HomePod 3Next-generation full-size HomePod with faster hardware and Siri AI supportIn development, but reportedly not imminent
HomePod TouchHomePod with a built-in 6-inch touchscreen.Uncertain; no firm launch window
Robotic home screen Display mounted on a robotic arm 2027 or beyond
Security cameraApple-designed home security cameraTiming uncertain

 






Why have Apple’s new Home products taken so long?
Apple’s next generation of smart-home products appears to have been delayed largely because of Siri. The company was developing a much more capable version of Siri for Apple Intelligence, while the processors inside the current HomePod mini and second-generation HomePod weren’t designed to run Apple’s latest AI features.
That created a problem for new HomePod hardware. Apple was reportedly preparing products such as a new HomePod mini and smart home display around the capabilities of the redesigned assistant, but Siri’s delayed development meant the hardware couldn’t launch as originally expected.
That situation has now changed. Siri AI arrived with Apple’s OS 27 updates in September 2026, removing one of the main dependencies that had been holding back Apple’s smart-home plans. Recent reports suggest the HomePod mini 2 and Apple’s smart home display are among the products closest to release.
The full-size HomePod appears to be on a different timetable, however. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September that Apple is testing a new full-size HomePod with Siri AI support, but said it “doesn’t appear to be imminent.” That means we no longer expect the HomePod 3 to necessarily arrive alongside the HomePod mini 2.








HomePod mini 2 rumors
We’ll start off with the rumors about the HomePod mini 2. The HomePod mini is Apple’s smaller, more affordable smart speaker. The new model is expected to offer a new red color option, major processor upgrade and improved connectivity.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




When is the HomePod mini 2 expected to launch?
October 13, 2026
Apple introduced the original HomePod mini in November 2020, so it is now nearly six years old and overdue for an update.
Rumours of a successor have circulated for more than a year. In January 2025, reports suggested a launch toward the end of 2025, and Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman subsequently said that new HomePod mini and Apple TV models were expected in fall 2025. Those products never materialised.
Attention then shifted to spring 2026, with reports suggesting Apple’s new smart home devices would launch alongside its redesigned Siri. However, that timetable also slipped as Apple continued work on its AI-powered assistant.
The latest reports now point to an October 13, 2026 launch. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple has several smart home products that are nearly ready but is waiting for the redesigned Siri to ship with the OS 27 updates before introducing new hardware.
If those plans remain on schedule, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to launch alongside Apple’s broader refresh of its smart home lineup this fall, with most reports pointing to October.
What changes are coming to the HomePod mini 2?
Black, blue, green, pink, and white color finishes.
The current HomePod mini is available in Midnight, White, Blue, Yellow and Orange. In September, MacRumors spotted Apple code that revealed five colors for the new model: black, blue, green, pink, and white.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September 2025, that Apple has tested additional colors for the next-generation model, including red, but it appears that red didn’t make the final cut. 
Otherwise, the HomePod mini 2 is expected to retain the same compact, spherical design as the current model, with no major external changes rumored. Instead, Apple is reportedly focusing on upgraded internal hardware, including an S9 or newer chip capable of supporting Apple’s latest Siri AI features.
Other changes coming to HomePod mini 2
Beyond the color changes revealed in Apple code, the main expected hardware upgrade is a newer processor capable of supporting Siri AI. Reports also point to newer Apple networking and Ultra Wideband hardware, along with possible audio improvements.
Siri AI support: A newer processor should allow the HomePod mini 2 to support Apple’s latest Siri AI features, something the current S5-based model wasn’t designed for.
Improved connectivity: Reports have pointed to Apple’s newer in-house networking hardware, Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip.
Audio improvements: Apple is expected to upgrade the speaker’s audio hardware and processing.
Other internal upgrades: Further hardware refinements are possible.






HomePad/Smart Home Hub rumors
Possible launch: October 13, 2026, according to Bloomberg
Strategy: A new smart-home display category for Apple
HomePad release date 
Apple’s first smart home display could launch on October 13, 2026. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple plans to introduce its new smart-home products on that date, with the long-rumored home hub expected to be the centerpiece of the launch. 
There are signs that Apple could make an announcement even earlier. Confidential retail-display boxes have arrived in Apple Stores, reportedly marked for opening on October 8. This suggests that a product launch is imminent, although it is unclear what the materials relate to. The iPhone Duo goes on sale October 23, so October 8 would appear too early to be connected to that.
Apple has not confirmed the date, and Gurman’s report does not say whether the products will be unveiled at an event or announced through Apple’s website. 
The product had originally been expected earlier in 2026, but its launch was repeatedly pushed back while Apple completed the Siri AI technology that arrived with its September OS 27 updates. Gurman previously reported that the hardware had been ready for some time, with Siri the main reason for the delay.
Apple’s own software has also provided evidence that the product is approaching launch. References discovered in macOS identify J490/HomeAccessory17,1 and J491/HomeAccessory17,2, which are believed to correspond to the tabletop and wall-mounted versions of Apple’s smart home hub.
Earlier reports had only narrowed the launch window to 2026, while a March post from leaker Kosutami hinted at a fall release. Those reports have now been superseded by Gurman’s more specific October 13 timeframe.
What is the HomePad?
The HomePad – also referred to as Apple’s Smart Home Hub or home display – is expected to be a compact 6-inch smart display designed to act as a central interface for the home. It would combine Siri AI, smart-home controls, FaceTime, media playback and Apple services in a device intended to remain plugged in on a countertop, desk, bedside table or wall.
The latest reports suggest that it will be considerably smaller than many earlier concept images implied. A six-inch square display would measure only about 4.25 inches across each side, making it much more of a close-up personal device than an iPad-sized family display. It is likely to be more “desk scale” than “room scale.” 
Apple’s new Siri AI is expected to be central to the HomePad experience. Its delayed development appears to have been one of the main reasons the hardware did not launch earlier.

				
					

				
			
Foundry / ChatGPT




HomePad design, features and specs
Reported features include:
6-inch display: The latest Bloomberg report points to a six-inch display with rounded corners, making the device considerably smaller than many earlier renders suggested.
iMac G4-style tabletop design: The standard model is reportedly mounted above a circular metal speaker base on a polished metal arm, with a design said to be reminiscent of the classic iMac G4. 
Colors: Leaker itspdfu has suggested Rose Pink, Silver, Space Gray and Starlight based on Photo Face setup assets.
Tilting display: The screen is reportedly designed to tilt forward and backward manually.
Wall-mounted version: A second model is reportedly designed to mount on a wall, with a thin square base containing the speakers and microphones.
No battery: The device is expected to remain plugged in, reportedly using USB-C for power.
Siri AI: Apple’s new Siri technology is expected to be central to the device.
Smart-home controls: It should act as a central interface for Home accessories.
FaceTime and communication: A front-facing camera is expected to support FaceTime calls.
User recognition: The device is reportedly designed to recognize household members by face and voice, then display that person’s own calendar, reminders, notes and other information.
Visitor mode: Reports suggest it will be able to hide personal information when guests are using the device.
iPhone authentication: A nearby iPhone may be used for stronger authentication when required.
Other software clues and reports suggest the device could also offer:
Apple apps and services: Reports specifically mention Calendar, Messages, Photos, FaceTime, Notes, Reminders, Music, Podcasts and smart-home controls.
Entertainment: The device is also expected to function as an entertainment hub for streaming music and video, as well as making FaceTime calls via a built-in camera.
New home-focused software: The device is reportedly running a new interface combining elements of Apple Watch, Apple TV and iPhone/iPad software, including widgets, clock faces and photo displays rather than simply running iPadOS. 
No App Store expected at launch: Current reports do not mention an App Store, suggesting the HomePad may initially operate more like a dedicated smart-home appliance than a general-purpose iPad.
Other clues about HomePad software:
Kitchen integration: A new “CookingKit” framework and expanded food sections in Apple News indicate that kitchen assistance, such as searching for recipes by ingredient, could be a primary selling point.
Advanced home control: Code found in the iOS 26 Home app describes an “Adaptive Temperature” feature, which could allow the HomePad to offer more granular control over smart thermostats, including energy-saving optimizations based on local electricity rates.






HomePod 3 rumors
The larger HomePod is more expensive than the HomePod mini, delivering richer, louder audio with deeper bass and spatial audio. The next generation is expected to get a processor upgrade, improved connectivity and better sound.

				
					

				
			
Michael Brown/Foundry




When is the HomePod 3 expected to launch?
Release date: Unknown; not expected imminently
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported in September 2026 that Apple was testing a new full-size HomePod with Siri AI support, but that the release did not appear to be imminent.
What changes are coming to the HomePod 3?
Unlike the HomePod mini 2, there are relatively few leaks about hardware upgrades coming to the full-size HomePod. However, it’s expected to receive the same core internal upgrades needed to support Apple’s AI ambitions.
Expected improvements include: 
More powerful chip: The current HomePod uses the S7 chip from the Apple Watch Series 7. A next-generation model is expected to adopt a significantly faster Apple silicon chip, potentially the S9 or newer, to support Apple Intelligence features.
Siri AI support: The upgraded hardware should allow the HomePod to run Apple’s new Siri AI features that aren’t supported by the current S7-based model.
Improved Connectivity: Rumours point to Apple’s in-house networking chip, together with Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip for improved performance and smart home integration.
Audio Enhancements: Apple is also expected to refine the speaker system with upgraded drivers and audio processing.
In September, a post by itspdfu, who has a history of posting leaks online, said that audioOS27, the operating system for HomePod devices, supports Siri AI. The same source claimed that a future HomePod could also include new animations for its top display.
Beyond these internal upgrades, some reports suggest Apple is experimenting with a HomePod featuring a built-in display. That device is expected to be a separate product rather than a standard HomePod 3, and we cover those rumours in the next section.






HomePod with touchscreen (HomePod Touch) rumors
Apple has been rumored to be working on a HomePod with a screen for years, although exactly what form that product will take remains unclear. Older reports have described a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated touchscreen, sometimes referred to unofficially as a “HomePod Touch.”
There is considerable uncertainty here because some older reports about a “HomePod with a display” may describe the same product that more recent reports characterize as Apple’s HomePad or smart home hub. We are treating the HomePod Touch separately here only where reports specifically describe a HomePod-style speaker with an integrated screen.
That is a little more internally consistent and makes the distinction from the HomePad clear without implying that the HomePod Touch is definitely a separate product.





				
					

				
			
Foundry and Apple




When could the touchscreen HomePod launch?
Possible launch: Unknown
Apple has been working on redesigning the HomePod to include a display for some time. Back in March 2023, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo claimed Apple would “unveil a redesigned HomePod featuring a 7-inch panel.” Kuo initially expected this product to arrive in the first half of 2024, but that timeline slipped. In December 2024, he reported further delays had pushed the launch to after WWDC 2025, citing software development challenges. Then, in March 2025, Kuo suggested the device had been delayed again, due to Apple Intelligence setbacks.
Those predictions have all passed without a product appearing. Siri AI has since arrived, but there is currently no firm report giving this touchscreen HomePod a new launch date. It is therefore possible that earlier reports referred to a product that has evolved, been delayed further, or overlaps with Apple’s separately reported HomePad project.

				
					

				
			
HomePod with display incoming?

Foundry




What could the touchscreen HomePod be like?
Display size: 6 and 7-inch touchscreens.
Software: Custom touchscreen operating system running apps like Weather, Calendar, Photos, HomeKit as well as Apple Music
One of the biggest limitations of today’s HomePod is that almost every interaction relies on Siri. A built-in display would provide a more direct way to control music, manage smart home devices and access information, putting Apple’s device in direct competition with the Amazon Echo Show and Google Nest Hub.
According to current rumours, Apple’s display-equipped HomePod will feature a 6-7-inch touchscreen and run a touch-optimised version of homeOS, allowing it to function as both a smart speaker and a smart home hub. Unlike existing HomePods, it is expected to use a far more powerful A-series chip – possibly an A18 or similar – to support Apple’s redesigned AI-powered Siri and the more demanding graphical interface.
Rumoured features:
Large touchscreen: A 6-7-inch display for controlling smart home devices, viewing photos, checking the weather, following recipes and interacting with apps.
Powerful Apple silicon: An A-series chip is expected to replace the S-series processor used in current HomePods, providing the performance needed for Apple Intelligence and the touchscreen interface.
Smart-home controls: A touchscreen HomePod would logically offer easier access to Home controls, although reports about apps and a dedicated smart-home interface may refer instead to Apple’s separate HomePad project
Improved connectivity: Apple’s in-house networking chip, Wi-Fi 6E and an upgraded Ultra Wideband chip are all rumoured.
FaceTime camera: Reports suggest Apple may include a built-in camera for FaceTime and other video-based features. These could instead relate to Apple’s separate HomePad project.
Possible modular design: Some less-established reports have suggested that a display could dock with a speaker base. This has not been corroborated by the more recent reports describing Apple’s HomePad.
If accurate, this would represent Apple’s biggest expansion of the HomePod lineup since its debut, transforming it from a voice-first speaker into a full smart home controller.

				
					

				
			Amazon Echo Show beside the HomePod mini, 
Ben Patterson/Foundry




Apple robotic home display rumors
Possible launch: 2027 or later
Strategy: A premium smart-home device with a movable display
Apple is also developing a much more ambitious smart-home device that shouldn’t be confused with the HomePad expected first (see above).
As far back as April 2021, Mark Gurman described a high-end device combining a HomePod speaker, a touchscreen, and a camera mounted on a robotic arm that could follow the user around the room during video calls. Gurman has made various references to this over the years.
The device, previously identified as J595, is reportedly an iPad-like display attached to a motorized robotic arm. The arm would allow the screen to move and reposition itself, potentially following a person around the room during FaceTime calls or turning toward whoever is speaking.
Bloomberg has described it as a higher-end smart-home command center that could combine videoconferencing, home controls and security functions. Unlike the stationary HomePad, this appears to be a significantly more complex—and probably more expensive—product. Earlier reports have suggested a price that could reach around $1,000.
The robotic display is also believed to be further away than the HomePad. Previous reports placed it in late 2026 or 2027 at the earliest, and Apple’s more recent software leaks have focused on the J490 and J491 stationary home hubs rather than J595.
What could the robotic display do?
Reported capabilities include:
A large display mounted on a motorized arm.
Automatically turning toward the person using it.
FaceTime and other video calling.
Siri AI and smart-home controls.
Cameras and gesture recognition
Reports suggest cameras could support FaceTime, security monitoring and potentially recognition of users or gestures. Apple has also previously filed patents describing HomePod-related gesture controls, although patents do not necessarily indicate features destined for a shipping product.






What chips will power the new HomePods?
The biggest limitation of today’s HomePods isn’t their speakers – it’s their processors. The HomePod mini still uses the Apple Watch S5 chip introduced in 2019, while the second-generation HomePod runs on the newer, but still relatively modest, S7 chip from the Apple Watch Series 7.
Those chips are powerful enough for music playback, Home controls and existing Siri functions, but they were not designed to run the new Siri AI capabilities introduced with Apple’s OS 27 generation.
That hardware gap helps explain why Apple is expected to introduce new HomePod hardware rather than bringing the full Siri AI experience to the existing models.
HomePod mini 2 & HomePod 3
Gurman has said the main hardware change he has specifically reported for the new HomePods is a faster chip, although he has not identified which processor Apple will use.
HomePod with a screen
The display-equipped HomePod is expected to require substantially more processing power than Apple’s existing smart speakers. Because it will reportedly run a touch-based operating system alongside Apple Intelligence, most analysts expect it to use an A-series processor, with an A17 Pro or A18 among the leading predictions. Apple has not confirmed the chip, and these reports remain speculative.
Whatever processors Apple ultimately chooses, the goal appears to be the same across the entire HomePod range: replacing ageing Apple Watch chips with modern Apple silicon capable of delivering the full Apple Intelligence experience.






New HomePod Prices
The prices for the HomePods increased in June 2026:
HomePod: $349/£349 (was $299/£299)
HomePod mini: $129/£129 (was $99/£99)
Apple raised HomePod prices in June 2026, so we wouldn’t expect the new models to return automatically to the previous $99/$299 price points.
However, a HomePod with a built-in screen could command a higher price. It may launch as a separate product altogether, potentially starting around $399/£399, or higher, depending on features.






Buying advice: Should you wait or buy a HomePod now? 
Wait if: You are considering a HomePod mini. A replacement now appears close, with reports pointing to fall 2026 and Apple code already revealing the unreleased model.
Buy now if: You need a HomePod immediately and find a worthwhile discount. The current HomePod and HomePod mini still work well as speakers and smart-home hubs, but their older processors mean they aren’t designed for Apple’s newer Siri AI capabilities.
If you want a screen: Wait. Apple’s first dedicated home display appears much closer than the more speculative touchscreen HomePod.






What is on Apple’s Smart Home Roadmap
September 2026: Apple’s OS 27 generation introduced its new Siri AI capabilities, removing one of the major software dependencies that had reportedly delayed Apple’s new home hardware.
Fall 2026: The HomePod mini 2 is expected, with October currently the leading possibility.
Fall 2026: Apple’s HomePad/smart home display could also launch, although its timing is less certain.
Beyond 2026: A new full-size HomePod is being tested, but Bloomberg reports that it does not appear imminent.
2027 or later: Apple’s more ambitious robotic home display could follow.
Timing unknown: Apple is also reportedly developing home-security camera hardware.

title: Apple’s home hub isn’t what you think it is
content:
Macworld





Apple may be less than two weeks away from releasing an all-new product in a new device category: a smart home hub. The device is said to be the start of a big push into the smart home category, which Apple has really only dabbled with so far. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman says Apple is finally set to announce it on October 13, after years of waiting for the new Siri AI to arrive, which will play a central role in the new device.
According to the most reliable leaks and rumors, this is what we know of the device’s design and operation:
It will have a square aspect ratio with rounded corners and a 6-inch (diagonal) display.
It won’t have a battery, relying instead on USB-C for power.
It will have a metal, round base with perforated holes for the speakers and microphones.
It will attach to the countertop base via a polished metal arm, “reminiscent” of the classic iMac G4.
It will have a single front-facing FaceTime camera.
Additionally, the device is said to run on a new operating system that combines the “StandBy” type widgets and display of the iPhone, screens and faces like the Apple Watch, and some of the media capabilities of Apple TV. A secondary version that mounts to a wall is said to be in the works, too.
There will be clocks and photo displays, of course, but the device will primarily control smart home devices via a Home app of sorts, and include Apple Music, Calendar, Podcasts, Messages, FaceTime, News, Notes, and Reminders. There is no reported mention of an App Store, so it appears as though this is an accessory rather than a standalone platform.
A core feature is said to be user recognition. Since this is meant to be stationary in your home and not portable, it has to work for all the people in your house. So it recognizes people via their face and voice, and then customizes the display to their own preferences, showing their own data and accessing their own calendar, notes, reminders, and so on. 
But if you’re expecting an iPad-like experience, think again.
A tiny 6-inch display
Apple sites like ours have been reporting on this so-called HomePad for ages. Apple has had it more or less ready to go for a long time, but it will rely on Siri for use, and Siri only just got its big brain transplant, so the home hub has sat on the back burner. We’ve largely envisioned a larger device that can act as a centerpiece of a room, something like an iPad or a small iMac.
But based on the latest rumors, most of the renders and mock-ups you see online have the scale all wrong, and it may have given you the wrong impression of its size.

				
					

				
			Macrumors
Over at MacRumors, you will have seen the above mockup, with the square screen over what looks a lot like an iMac G4 base. There’s no scale present, so of course it could be tiny, but the size of the text and number of tiles on the screen makes it seem like it’s hovering over a big iMac G4-like base. That makes the display appear closer to 8-10 inches on a side, or maybe 12 inches diagonal.

				
					

				
			9to5Mac
Mockups like this one from 9to5Mac are common, too, with a display (in this case not square) on top of a standard HomePod. The regular HomePod is 5.6 inches wide. So this mockup shows a screen at least 7 inches wide, or 8.75 inches diagonal.
A square display with a diagonal measurement of 6 inches is only 4.25 inches on each side. That’s only about 1.5 times as wide as an iPhone 18 Pro. Amazon’s Echo Show and Google Nest Hub are both larger than six inches and have widescreen displays. The HomePad will seem minuscule by comparison.

				
					

				
			
This ChatGPT-generated image of Apple’s upcoming smart home hub gives an idea of how small it might be, according to rumors.

Foundry / ChatGPT




Our shameless AI-generated mockup shows what that would look like to scale. Perhaps the base will be a HomePod mini-like half-dome. Maybe it will be more of fat, round coaster. But a rounded-square 6-inch display is really rather small—for comparison, a regular iPhone is more than 30 percent taller!
This scale makes some sense, especially if Apple is trying to make this an affordable device where you buy several and scatter them around the house. But it also speaks to how Apple intends its customers to use it.
How might you use it?
A square display that is only six inches diagonal makes this device much more like an iPhone on a stick than an iPad, or even an iPad mini. That really limits its usefulness for large rooms. This isn’t the kind of thing you can hope to read while standing 10 feet away or hold FaceTime calls from across your living room. It’s more personal than that.
The ability to use it in the kitchen is going to depend very much on the size of your kitchen and where you put it. With enlarged text, you might be able to read a recipe from five or six feet away, but not much more than that. FaceTime calls are really only going to feel good when you’re right up near it. On the other hand, this becomes the perfect little gadget to sit on your bedside table, working as a smart alarm clock, noise machine, and podcast speaker.
While it doesn’t really make sense as an “across the living room” device, it would fit nicely on the end table next to your couch. It seems to be something that’s a little easier to ignore when you’re not using it, rather than a centerpiece. More like a HomePod mini than an iMac in that way.
It also means the base will be of limited size, and that puts limits on the sound volume and quality. Don’t expect the room-filling sound of the big HomePod, but rather something best for podcasts, audiobooks, or music at a modest volume and close distance.
Of course, we won’t really know what it looks like or how big it is until Apple announces it. The rumors about its design have been remarkably consistent over the last couple of years, but we don’t have leaked CAD drawings or parts from parts suppliers or anything like that to go from to know the scale. If the rumors are accurate, you should expect this home hub to be something “desk scale” rather than “room scale.”

title: Microsoft 365 Work Accounts May Stop Syncing in Apple Mail
content:
From October 1, 2026, Microsoft began disabling Exchange Web Services (EWS) by default in Exchange Online, which will cut off the protocol that Apple's Mail and Calendar apps on Mac still rely on to sync Microsoft 365 work accounts.


The cutoff has been on the cards for a fairly long time, as Microsoft stopped adding new features to EWS back in 2018, while in 2023 it announced that it would start disabling the protocol in Exchange Online from October 2026.

recently updated post from June, Microsoft described the change as a "phased rollout," so some Mac users could lose access sooner than others.

It's still possible for IT administrators to restore access. However, Microsoft plans to shut down EWS in Exchange Online permanently on April 1, 2027, and no extensions are currently planned.

support document, the company says it is "actively working with Microsoft" to move Mail, Calendar, Contacts, Notes, and Reminders apps on Mac to the newer Microsoft Graph API in a future macOS 27 update.

Except, that update hasn't arrived yet. Apple skipped macOS 27.1 betas entirely, while release notes for the macOS 27.2 betas have yet to make any mention of Graph support.

Meanwhile, affected organizations can just keep EWS running or move Mac users to a Graph-compatible client, such as Microsoft's Outlook app.

Note that the change will only affect Microsoft's cloud-hosted email server. In other words, companies that run their own Exchange servers aren't affected. Neither will iPhone and iPad be impacted, since they use Exchange ActiveSync rather than EWS.

(Thanks, Jonathan!)
